newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE - Ex-actor eyes Philippine presidency. [CORRECTED 03:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ex-actor eyes Philippine presidency. [CORRECTED 03:43 GMT]

text.p: A former movie actor who has a reputation as a clown, heavy drinker and philanderer, a son accused of beating up an old woman and a job which makes him attend state dinners he hates, believes he can be president.

Vice-President Joseph Estrada (corrects first name from John) is convinced it is his destiny to lead the Philippines into the 21st century, and all major opinion polls seem to agree he is not merely day-dreaming.
"Being president is a destiny ... No amount of criticism can stop me," he told Reuters in an interview.
Estrada says he is used to people mocking his ambitions but his gut feeling is that he'll have the last laugh in what he claims will be "the last battle of my life".
The 1998 elections are likely to be crucial in helping decide whether the Philippines' economic comeback since President Fidel Ramos took office in 1992 proves more than just a flash in the pan.
One prominent local economist was recently reported as saying that Estrada -- known universally by the nickname "Erap" -- would be a disaster as president.
Erap refers to "pare" spelt backwards and in Tagalog can be loosely translated as "pal" or "mate".

Jitters are not just confined to financial markets, either. The polls have so alarmed the powerful Roman Catholic Church that the clergy is determined to pull out all stops to thwart Estrada's dreams, according to Manila newspaper reports.
To veteran political analyst Amando Doronila, an Estrada presidency would be like "a plague."
"Can this man represent (us) in the community of nations? Will anybody take him seriously?" commentator Paulyn Paredes Sicam wrote in the Manila Times.

Estrada used his popularity as an actor specialising in "tough guy" roles fighting for the oppressed to win election as mayor of the Manila suburb of San Juan in 1972. He was elected senator in 1987 and vice president in 1992.

Ramos appointed him to head a commission charged with hunting down bank robbers, drug pushers and kidnappers. Estrada and his agents wiped out some major gangs but allegations that his men had summarily executed suspects prompted Ramos to clip their powers last year.
If elected, Estrada says his main priority will be law and order. He vows to raise police salaries to discourage corruption, and jail judges and policemen who do not resist temptation.
He denied using his influence to get one of his sons off the hook after the young man was accused of beating up an old woman in a highly publicised scandal.
Estrada, 59, modelled himself on James Dean and Marlon Brando when he was a young actor and still wears his hair in a 1950s-style quiff, despite an unglamorous waistline.
Critics put down a Brandoesque slur in his speech to boozing but Estrada insists that is a thing of the past.
Estrada believes his popularity is rooted among the millions of poor Filipinos who identify with his down-to-earth manner.
"I hate attending state affairs, state dinners...It's all a fake," he said.
Dining with diplomats, he is sometimes seized with a desire to eat with his hands, as many Filipinos routinely do.
In a country where politicians are largely viewed as corrupt, Estrada has not been tainted by accusations of corruption.
His renowned escapades with women, he insisted, all happened when he was still in the movies, "where women come easy ... I have mellowed already".

He fumed at suggestions that he was an economic ignoramus. The "Estrada economic vision," he said, is spelt out in a programme top economists have drafted for him, made up of simple, achievable attempts to lessen the poverty around him.
It calls for maintaining Ramos' economic policies while paying more attention to agriculture by building extra farm-to-market roads and more rural banks for soft loans.
Estrada admits he is no intellectual but claims intellectuals have got the country nowhere. It is time, he says, to try a man who will rule with plain "common sense".

"When I ran for mayor the rich people here, the professionals, laughed at me. But the poor people, those who live in the slums, the taxi drivers, the domestic helpers, these were the people who voted for Erap," he said.
"When I ran for senator, these were the people who carried me. Whoever Erap is now is because of them."
